title: The MGA and Cru System Explained
quiz.0.question: In which year did the Barolo MGA system officially come into force?
quiz.0.explanation: The Barolo MGA system came into force in 2010, with 170 vineyards recognised as MGAs.
quiz.1.question: Which MGA does Giacomo Conterno's flagship Monfortino come from?
quiz.1.explanation: Monfortino comes from Giacomo Conterno's Cascina Francia vineyard in Serralunga d'Alba — the Francia MGA (about 6 ha, owned solely by Conterno); Vigna Rionda is a separate legendary MGA in Serralunga.
quiz.2.question: How many official MGAs does Barbaresco have?
quiz.2.explanation: Barbaresco has 66 official MGAs, far fewer than Barolo's 170.
quiz.3.question: When an MGA is shown on a label, what restriction applies to the size of its name?
quiz.3.options.0: No larger than the producer's name
quiz.3.options.1: No larger than the appellation name
quiz.3.explanation: The rules state that the MGA name may not be larger than the appellation name (e.g. Barolo), to avoid misleading consumers.
slides.0.title: The MGA and Cru System Explained
slides.0.subtitle: The precise terroir code of Barolo & Barbaresco
slides.1.title: What Is an MGA? How It Differs from a French Cru
slides.1.content:
MGA = Menzioni Geografiche Aggiuntive (additional geographical mentions)

MGA is an official term in Italian wine law that lets producers name a smaller geographical unit on the label, stating exactly where the grapes come from. It came into force in Barbaresco in 2007 and in Barolo in 2010; Barolo has 170 vineyard MGAs (plus 11 village MGAs) and Barbaresco has 66.

MGA vs the French Burgundy cru system

The Burgundy cru system

  • History: began in the 13th century, evolving over centuries
  • Classification: Grand Cru → Premier Cru → Village (an official quality ranking)
  • Grand Cru: 33 (a globally recognised mark of quality)
  • Market recognition: the highest in the world

The Barolo MGA system

  • History: in force since 2010 (very new)
  • Classification: geographical mention only, no official quality ranking
  • Number of MGAs: 170 (far more than Burgundy)
  • Market recognition: accepted by professionals, unfamiliar to ordinary consumers
slides.2.title: The Terroir of Barolo's Five Great Villages
slides.2.content:
Serralunga d'Alba

Structure | Serravallian (formerly Helvetian) calcareous marl and sandstone

The firmest tannins / needs the longest ageing / top sites: Vigna Rionda, Francia, Lazzarito / dried rose, tar

La Morra

Elegance | Tortonian marl (Sant'Agata fossil marls)

The most aromatic and delicate / earlier drinking / top sites: Brunate, Cerequio, Rocche dell'Annunziata / rose, red berries

Barolo village

Balance | mixed soils (marl + sand)

Elegance and power combined / the longest history / top sites: Cannubi (1752), Sarmassa / refined tannins

Castiglione Falletto

Classic | complex mixed soils

Powerful, complex, long-lived / top sites: Monprivato (Giuseppe Mascarello), Villero, Bricco Boschis / smoke and minerals
slides.3.title: Legendary MGAs in Depth
slides.3.content:
Cannubi — The Heart of Barolo (Barolo village, 1752)

Soils: Tortonian marl with sand (well drained) | Elevation 250-300 m | Facing south/south-east
Style: delicate and elegant (not powerful) | rose petal, red cherry, liquorice | ages 20-40 years
Top names: Luciano Sandrone, Chiara Boschis E.Pira, Brezza

Vigna Rionda — Serralunga's Legend (Serralunga d'Alba)

Soils: Serravallian calcareous marl and sandstone | Elevation 300-360 m | Facing south/south-west
Style: one of Barolo's most powerful and complex | black fruit, tar, rose, minerals | ages 30-50 years
Top names: Massolino (Vigna Rionda Riserva), Oddero, Luigi Pira
slides.4.title: Barbaresco's Three Legendary Crus
slides.4.content:
Barbaresco vs Barolo at a Glance

Size: about 750 ha (vs Barolo about 2,200 ha) | MGAs: 66 (vs 170) | Ageing: 26 months (vs 38)
Style: Barbaresco is more elegant and delicate, ready earlier | Barolo is more powerful and structured, needing long ageing | top Barbaresco is usually more affordable than Barolo of a similar level

Three Legendary Crus

🌹 Asili (Barbaresco village) — queen of elegance: marl soils, rose + red berries + minerality, ages 15-30 years | Bruno Giacosa, Produttori del Barbaresco Riserva
💪 Rabajà (Barbaresco village) — king of power: calcareous marl with sand, blackberry + tar + leather, firm structure, ages 20-35 years | Bruno Rocca
💎 Pajé (Barbaresco village) — the crown of complexity: marl, red berries + flowers + minerals + truffle, balanced and elegant | Roagna
slides.5.title: How to Read an MGA Label
slides.5.content:
When buying Barolo/Barbaresco, an MGA label carries a wealth of information. Here are four key reading tips:

100% origin guarantee: for a wine naming an MGA, 100% of the grapes must be grown within that MGA, and the MGA may not be printed larger than the appellation name (e.g. BAROLO), to avoid misleading consumers
Producer before MGA: the same MGA interpreted by different producers can vary hugely in style. A top producer's "ordinary" MGA often beats a second-rate producer's top MGA
Vintage matters hugely: Nebbiolo depends greatly on vintage. Top vintages: 2016, 2013, 2010, 2006, 2004. A top MGA in an ordinary year is not necessarily better than a basic wine from a great year
Avoid the most famous MGAs: Cannubi and Vigna Rionda carry a high premium; other MGAs in the same village are often far more affordable, and top Barbaresco crus are usually more affordable than Barolo of a similar level
slides.6.title: 🍷 MGA Label Example: Barbaresco "Valeirano"
slides.6.caption: Ada Nada Barbaresco Valeirano DOCG 2008 — "Valeirano" is the MGA vineyard name, clearly printed no larger than the appellation name "BARBARESCO", as the rules require.
slides.7.title: 🍷 MGA Label Example: Barolo "Bricco Rocca"
slides.7.caption: Mario Olivero Barolo "Bricco Rocca" — not as famous as Cannubi or Vigna Rionda, but it shows the same MGA labelling rule: the vineyard name sits below the appellation name in smaller type.
slides.8.title: Key Takeaways
slides.8.points.0: MGA (Menzioni Geografiche Aggiuntive) is Italy's official system of geographical mentions, brought into force in 2007 (Barbaresco) and 2010 (Barolo)
slides.8.points.1: Barolo has 170 MGAs across 11 villages; Barbaresco has 66 MGAs
slides.8.points.2: The Burgundy crus have an official quality ranking (Grand Cru > Premier Cru); Barolo MGAs are geographical mentions only, with no quality ranking
slides.8.points.3: Barolo's five great villages: Serralunga (structure), La Morra (elegance), Barolo village (balance), Castiglione Falletto (classic), Monforte d'Alba (power and longevity)
slides.8.points.4: Cannubi is Barolo's oldest documented vineyard name (a 1752 record), elegant and delicate
slides.8.points.5: Vigna Rionda is one of Serralunga's most powerful terroirs; Giacomo Conterno's Monfortino comes from the Francia MGA in the same village
slides.8.points.6: Barbaresco's three legendary crus: Asili (elegance), Rabajà (power), Pajé (complexity), usually more affordable than Barolo of a similar level
slides.8.points.7: MGA labelling rules: 100% of the grapes from that site, and the MGA no larger than the appellation name
slides.8.points.8: Buying strategy: top producer > top vintage > top MGA; no need to chase the most famous MGAs
